My design would be a hybrid between the Real Time Strategy (RTS) and Multiplayer Online Battle Arena (MOBA) genres.

Instead of controlling heroes and having lanes filled with passive minions autoattacking each other to death, you would control your own armies and build unit production buildings in your base.

The game is played on a typical 3-lane map similar to games like DOTA 2 and League of Legends. The map has three towers per lane, a central command building which has to be destroyed in order to win the game, a jungle filled with monsters, and an epic boss within the jungle.

Landing the last-hit on a tower nets you a decent amount of money for yourself, and increases the passive income your team gains.

The game is 5v5 and has a blind pick mode where pretty much "anything goes" (you can pick any faction you want, regardless of who else is playing it) and a draft pick mode where playable factions get banned and picked in team order.

This game would also be free-to-play and operate on a 'pay to go faster' model whereby you get a free rotation of factions each week and can buy factions either with in-game currency or real money. Cosmetic skins would also be available for money.

Some of the factions I thought of in this game include:

  • Mercs - They rely on small, mobile and specialized infantry forces. Units are specialized on damage, support, tanking and even a mine-layer for limited zone control. Their strength is in their mobility and power, although their units are expensive. Mercs are generally all-rounded for offence and defence and can perform well in all stages of the game.

  • Hive - The Hive are a hornet-like race that rely on overwhelming their foes through large numbers of ground and air units. Their armies are relatively cheap and mobile, but weak. Their high tier options are also quite limited and expensive to produce. Playing Hive generally relies on taking map control early for your team and maximising income for yourself through control of the jungle or lanes so that you can shit monstrosities in the late game.

  • Primal - A galactic civilization of giants which favours offensive play. Primal society has resulted in the use of halflings (which are half-Primal offspring produced as a result of sex slavery, because Primals see other humanoid species as inferior and will enslave them after annexing their worlds) as infantry. Generally, actual Primals are expensive, elite units which require you to progress up the tech tree to produce.

  • Underworld - With a heavy focus on defensive yet mobile play, the forces of the Underworld generally rely on their necromantic abilities to raise the dead as soldiers and spread their blight across the map. They generally play like a mix between SC2 Zerg and WC3 Undead. It is ill advised to engage Underworld forces on desecrated ground because it gives them a sizeable boost in power.

  • Imperials - The Imperial Empire spans multiple stars and is ruled from its home planet, Earth. They primarily focus on immobile and defensive play using expensive and high-tech units such as tanks, tank destroyers, fighter jets, infantry donning power armour, battle-mechs, etc.

An Animal Crossing/Harvest Moon/Etrian Odyssey hybrid city builder.

Here's the premise: You start with a small village, and, as mayor, grow it into a large(ish) city. The scale never gets huge, but you are responsible for things like zoning, roads, by-laws, construction permits, things like that. However, you also play in this world and have to make a living. On top of being mayor, will you grow crops on the old abandoned farm outside town? or will you open up a trading post and sell others goods? Will you fish? Hunt monsters? or trade with far away places? It's up to you!

Game play would feature 2 modes: City mode, and personal mode. Personal mode you run around in the town, running your business, talking to townspeople, living life. City mode is akin to Cities: Skylines, though on a much smaller scale.

The game is on a mix of real time and fast time, the day/night cycle, match our own, but things like crops grow in mere minutes, when they would take months in real life. Seasons, unlike in real life would last a span of 1 week per season, eliminating the necessity for time skipping for season-exclusive items or crops.

You can also adopt pets. These pets would be monster-like creatures found in and around the town. Some are aggressive, others passive, some friendly. You can gather their eggs, hatch and breed them to either sell as livestock, pets or helpers around your business. You can also fight these monsters for fun and profit in the endless dungeon outside town, or send yours to fight in passive tournaments.

Multi-player would be incorporated. You can invite other players into your town, trade with them on a global marketplace (See Guild Wars 2 Trading Post for example), or battle against them.

The game would have a lot of elements, but as a long term game, it needs to have lots of options.

A city "fixing" game. It will contain real cities from around the world that have big problems with them. Like Jakarta, Indonesia for example. In real life, it has piles of garbage here and there. It has open sewers, problematic traffic (due to density, but also due to poorly designed roads in most areas), corrupt police, government workers too lazy to do their jobs, it heavily floods in many places of the city every year, etc. The biggest problem, though, seems to be the trash. It gets piled up near sidewalks, in the rivers/lakes (The rivers don't even flow anymore), and just wherever is convenient.

The goal of the game is to get rid of these problems. There wouldn't really be any building mechanic to it. You'd just make policies to take care of these problems. It's not so easy, though. One of the problems in the city is that barely anybody pays their taxes, and the government there doesn't have much ability to enforce the collection of them. The taxes they do manage to collect mostly gets embezzled too.

Run a garbage campaign. Right now, the government just pays random individuals to gather garbage by hand and carry them somewhere better. That's not very efficient as you may guess. In the game, you'd have to campaign for people to throw their trash in a designated garbage bin instead of just littering. Have them recycle. Invest in a fleet of garbage trucks. Somehow get all the trash out of the lakes and rivers.

That's the sort of game I would make if I had the money or talent.

Uber to drivers: We may pay you to work for us, but that doesn't make you employees

Yeah Uber, it kind of does.

Edit: I'm curious if this is some attempt to legal their way out of paying for certain employee benefits?
This lists the criteria to distinguish between an employee and a contractor: http://employment.findlaw.com/hiring-process/being-an-independent-contractor-vs-employee.html
Yup, though IIRC, that body of law was mainly Federal, so the state agencies that want to make Uber drivers employees for unemployment and other purposes aren't strictly bound by it.

They are absolutely right. Uber drivers are 1099 independent contractors. When you are an Uber driver, you are self-employed. While this means you will have to pay both the employer and employee side of income tax, it also means you can deduct more things as business expenses.

Think of it this way, you are essentially an Uber franchise. You own the business that offers a for hire driver service (and at the same time function as the sole employee), and in exchange for a cut of YOUR profits, Uber allows you to use their name and their product/software.

Which is fine, so long as Uber treats them properly like contractors, the question is whether they are or are not.

Many companies today just love to hire contractors out the ass, while also having specific required working hours, scheduling, etc. that is not allowed for contractors. You don't get your cake and eat it too.

This case is a bit more complicated than many like to acknowledge. Presumably this is referencing appeals court because Uber drivers were recently deemed employees by the California Labor Commission. I like ride sharing services and use them frequently, but Uber plays pretty fast and loose with employee protection and that makes me uncomfortable. Here's the top comment from a Hacker News discussion regarding the decision to classify Uber drivers as employees in California:

Skimming through the doc, court findings are:
1) Drivers providing their own cars is not a strong factor - pizza delivery employees also drive their own cars.
2) Uber "control the tools that drivers use" by regulating the newness of the car.
3) Uber exercises extensive control over vetting and hiring drivers and requires extensive personal information from drivers.
4) Uber alone sets prices, and tipping is discouraged, so there is no mechanism for driver (as "contractor") to set prices.
5) Plaintiff driver only provided her time and car. "Plaintiff's work did not entail any 'managerial' skills that could affect profit or loss."
6) Drivers cannot subcontract (presumably negating Uber's position as a "lead generation" tool for contractors).
Sorry that these are out of order. Look on Page 9 of court documents for full text.

In particular I think the inability to subcontract is what really sets Uber drivers apart from other 1099s.
